evidence.label: An explicit counterexample to the Auslander-Reiten conjecture
A counterexample to Tachikawa's second conjecture

headline: A module with no self-extensions in any degree can still fail to be projective, against Auslander–Reiten and Tachikawa.
scope: The examples are finite-dimensional algebras over one field of characteristic 2 with three free parameters, and every larger field. The commutative case stays open.
plain: In module theory, projective modules are the basic building blocks. The Auslander–Reiten conjecture says a module with no extensions to itself or to the algebra, in any degree, must be projective. Two papers claim this is false, using algebras over a field where 1 + 1 = 0. One counterexample also refutes Tachikawa's second conjecture. A derived algebra then refutes several Nakayama-type conjectures as well.
doesNot: This does not settle the commutative version of these conjectures.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Maurice Auslander and Idun Reiten, “On a generalized version of the Nakayama conjecture”
scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proofs hold, they disprove a cluster of conjectures central to the representation theory of algebras since the 1970s.

explanation:
The heart of the proof is a small two-by-two table of numbers. Its rows are H₁ to the power −m, then 1, and H₂ to the power −m, then 1. Its determinant is H₁^(−m) − H₂^(−m). The table can be undone exactly when that is not zero. As a stand-in, try H₁ = 2 and H₂ = 3. For m = 1, 2, 3 the determinant is 1/6, 5/36 and 19/216. It is never zero, because a power of 2 never equals the same power of 3.

Now try H₁ = −1 and H₂ = 1. For m = 2 the determinant is 1 − 1 = 0, and the table cannot be undone. The ratio −1 returns to 1 after two steps. The paper picks H₁ and H₂ whose ratio never returns to 1[10]. Then the table can be undone for every m at once[9]. That is what removes every obstruction in the proof.

Some words first. An algebra here is a finite-dimensional space of numbers with a multiplication, such as square matrices. A module is something the algebra acts on, like vectors under matrices. Projective modules are the basic building blocks: pieces of free copies of the algebra. Ext groups measure the ways two modules can be glued together, one for each degree 1, 2, 3, and so on.

The Auslander–Reiten conjecture asks this. If a module has no gluings with itself or with the algebra, in any positive degree, must it be projective[1]? It comes from Maurice Auslander and Idun Reiten's 1975 work on the generalized Nakayama conjecture[2]. It was proved in many cases. These include large classes of commutative rings[7]. They also include algebras whose radical cubed is zero[6]. Schulz found a module with no self-gluings, but over a skew field, outside this setting[8].

The first paper claims a counterexample[3]. The field is built from arithmetic where 1 + 1 = 0, extended by three independent unknowns q, H₁ and H₂. Over it the paper builds a finite-dimensional algebra and a module Z. The module is not projective, yet all its positive-degree gluings with itself and with the algebra vanish[3]. Z is also Gorenstein-projective, so a second conjecture about such modules fails too[4]. The examples survive every enlargement of the field[5].

How do the gluings vanish? The paper starts from a ten-dimensional algebra whose gluings form a very sparse pattern. It twists that algebra in two ways, scaled by H₁ and by H₂. Each degree-3m gluing gets multiplied by H₁^(−m) or by H₂^(−m). The two-by-two table compares the two twists. Because it can always be undone, every gluing of positive degree cancels, while the module stays non-projective.

The second paper aims at a stricter target. A self-injective algebra is one where the algebra itself has a strong symmetry. Tachikawa's second conjecture says a module with no positive self-gluings over such an algebra must be projective[12]. The paper builds a symmetric algebra, a special self-injective kind, with such a module that is not projective[13]. The extra difficulty is that gluings in negative degrees must also vanish[17].

From this second example the paper builds another algebra. That algebra refutes the classical Nakayama conjecture[15]. It also refutes the Auslander–Gorenstein conjecture[14]. It refutes the Wakamatsu tilting conjecture too[16]. The commutative version of these questions is not settled by either construction[11].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked formal statements of both main counterexamples. For Auslander–Reiten, it includes the eight simple modules and survival under field extension. For Tachikawa, it covers the symmetric algebra and its module. Lean does not include the later Nakayama-type consequences. No specialist review of these papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proofs hold. Lean checks both main counterexamples, but not the Nakayama-type consequences. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: Something an algebra acts on, the way matrices act on vectors.
A basic building block: a piece split off from free copies of the algebra.
A measure of the ways two modules can be glued together, one for each degree.
An algebra that, as a module over itself, is both a building block and an injective module.
A self-injective algebra that matches its own dual space in a balanced way.
A module inside an endless exact chain of building blocks that stays exact after dualizing.
